title: Where things are
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: N + está + debajo de/al lado de/cerca de + N

rules.text: Where something or someone IS always takes estar: El libro está en la mesa, never *es en la mesa. This is M2's split at its most mechanical — no judgement is needed, because a location is a location. (One thing does take ser: an event, La fiesta es en mi casa. That is a place where something HAPPENS rather than a thing that sits somewhere, and this level does not teach it.)

One Spanish word covers three English ones. en is "on" (en la mesa), "in" (en la casa) and "at" (en el trabajo), and nothing in the sentence chooses between them — English is the language doing extra work here, not Spanish.

hay says that something EXISTS, and it never changes for number: Hay un libro en la mesa · Hay libros en la mesa. One shape for "there is" and "there are" both, and there is no plural of it — *hayn does not exist.

hay and está are one English "there is" doing two jobs. hay brings something new into the conversation and is followed by un, una or a bare plural — Hay una tienda cerca de aquí. está places something both speakers already know about, so it follows el, la, mi or a name — La tienda está cerca de mi casa. hay never takes el or la after it.

The compound prepositions all end in de, and the de is not optional: debajo de la mesa, al lado de la puerta, cerca de mi casa. English "under the table" has no "of" in it, which is exactly why the de is the piece that gets dropped.

Two contractions are obligatory, and only in front of el: a + el = al (voy al parque) and de + el = del (cerca del parque). Never *a el, never *de el. Nothing contracts in front of la, los or las — a la tienda, cerca de la casa.
dónde carries an accent for the same reason qué and cómo do: it is asking. The verb comes straight after it and nothing else may squeeze in — ¿Dónde está el baño?, not *¿Dónde el baño está?

The order is the thing, then está, then where it is: El libro está en la mesa. With hay it turns around — hay, then the thing, then where: Hay un libro en la mesa. Saying which one you mean puts it first; saying that it exists at all puts hay first.
aquí is "here" and needs nothing in front of it, but it still takes the de of a compound preposition when one is there: cerca de aquí is "near here".

estar answers two different questions with the same verb. With a place it answers "where" — Está en la mesa. With an adjective it answers "how" — Estoy bien (M2), Estoy cansado (M9). ser is not an option in either case.

sentences.display: El libro está en la mesa
sentences.cue: The book is on the table
sentences.glossEn: lit. "The book is-at in the table"
sentences.literal: The book is in/on the table

words.note: The all-purpose place word. English chooses between in, on and at; Spanish uses en for all three and lets the noun make it obvious — en la mesa (on it), en la casa (in it), en el trabajo (at it).
Table. Feminine: la mesa, las mesas.

sentences.trap: "The book is on the table" tempts es, because the book really is there and nothing about it feels temporary. Location is estar's, always: está en la mesa.
sentences.sound: ME-sa, with a clean s — Spanish never buzzes it into a z. en is short and light, and the sentence leans on the two a's at the end.

variations.display: El libro está en la casa
variations.cue: The book is in the house
variations.changed: same en, now translated "in"

variations.display: Los libros están en la mesa
variations.cue: The books are on the table
variations.changed: plural subject, so está becomes están

mistake.display: El libro es en la mesa
mistake.why: ser classifies what a thing is. Where it sits is estar: El libro está en la mesa.

sentences.usage: Telling someone where to find something.
sentences.mnemonic: Place = estar. No exceptions worth learning yet.

words.note: "Where", with the accent because it is asking — the same mark that separates M2's cómo from como and M4's qué from que. Unaccented donde is the joining word: la casa donde vivo.

sentences.trap: The verb comes before the thing: ¿Dónde está mi libro? English can say "where my book is" inside a longer sentence; a Spanish question keeps está glued to dónde.
sentences.sound: DÓN-de. The stress is on the first syllable, which is where it would fall anyway — the accent here is doing grammar, not pronunciation.

variations.display: ¿Dónde está Ana?
variations.cue: Where is Ana?
variations.changed: a person instead of a thing — same question

variations.display: ¿Dónde están mis libros?
variations.cue: Where are my books?
variations.changed: plural, so está becomes están

mistake.why: Asking where something is is asking about its place, so it is estar: ¿Dónde está mi libro?

sentences.usage: The question you will ask most often in a strange house.
sentences.mnemonic: dónde asks, donde joins — the mark is the question.

sentences.display: Hay un libro en la mesa
sentences.cue: There is a book on the table
sentences.glossEn: lit. "There-is a book on the table"
sentences.literal: There-is a book on the table

words.note: One word for both English phrases, and it never moves: hay un libro, hay libros, hay veinte libros. It says that something exists somewhere rather than saying where a known thing is — that job belongs to está.

sentences.trap: Two English "there is"es, two Spanish words. Use hay when you are announcing the book, and está when your listener already knows which book you mean.
sentences.sound: One syllable, and it sounds like English "eye" — the h is silent, as every Spanish h is.

variations.display: Hay libros en la mesa
variations.cue: There are books on the table
variations.changed: plural — and hay does not change at all

variations.display: ¿Hay una mesa en la casa?
variations.cue: Is there a table in the house?
variations.changed: as a question, with the marks doing the work

mistake.display: Hay el libro en la mesa
mistake.why: hay cannot take el or la. Say Hay un libro (announcing one) or El libro está en la mesa (placing the one you both mean).

sentences.usage: Announcing what is in a room.
sentences.mnemonic: hay for that it exists, está for where it is.

sentences.display: El libro está debajo de la mesa
sentences.cue: The book is under the table
sentences.glossEn: lit. "The book is-at underneath of the table"
sentences.literal: The book is underneath of the table

words.note: Two words that work as one preposition, and the de is not optional — English "under the table" has nothing there, so the de is what learners drop. In front of a masculine el it contracts: debajo del libro.

sentences.trap: *Debajo la mesa is the mistake this rule exists for. Every compound preposition here ends in de, and it stays whether English shows anything or not.
sentences.sound: de-BA-jo de. The j rasps from the back of the throat, like the ch in Scottish "loch", and the b between vowels is soft.

variations.display: El libro está debajo del pan
variations.cue: The book is under the bread
variations.changed: de + el = del in front of a masculine noun

variations.display: El pan está debajo de la mesa
variations.cue: The bread is under the table
variations.changed: swap what is hiding

mistake.display: El libro está debajo la mesa
mistake.why: The de is part of the preposition: debajo de la mesa.

sentences.usage: Where things go when you drop them.
sentences.mnemonic: Every one of them ends in de. Say the de.

sentences.display: Ana está al lado de la puerta
sentences.cue: Ana is next to the door
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Ana is-at to-the side of the door"
sentences.literal: Ana is at-the side of the door

words.note: Literally "at the side of", and all three words are fixed. The al inside it is already a + el, and the de at the end contracts the same way when a masculine el follows: al lado del baño.
Door. Feminine: la puerta. The ue in the middle is one glide, not two syllables.

sentences.trap: English says "next to" in two words and Spanish takes four bits — a, el, lado, de — of which the first two are already fused into al. Nothing here can be shortened.
sentences.sound: al LA-do de PUER-ta: the stress falls on LA and on PUER, and both r's are single taps rather than the English growl.

variations.display: Ana está al lado del baño
variations.cue: Ana is next to the bathroom
variations.changed: de + el = del, because baño is masculine

variations.display: La mesa está al lado de la puerta
variations.cue: The table is next to the door
variations.changed: swap what is beside it

mistake.display: Ana está al lado la puerta
mistake.why: The de holds the phrase to the noun: al lado de la puerta.

sentences.usage: Pointing someone at a person in a room.
sentences.mnemonic: al lado de — "at the side of", word for word.

sentences.display: La tienda está cerca de mi casa
sentences.cue: The shop is near my house
sentences.glossEn: lit. "The shop is-at near of my house"
sentences.literal: The shop is near of my house

words.note: The everyday word for a shop, understood everywhere Spanish is spoken. Feminine: la tienda.
"Near", and again the de is compulsory: cerca de mi casa. In front of a masculine el it becomes cerca del. Bare cerca on its own means "nearby", with nothing named after it.
House, and also home: en casa is "at home", with no article at all. Feminine: la casa.

sentences.trap: mi is enough on its own — mi casa, not *la mi casa. The possessive replaces the article rather than joining it.
sentences.sound: CER-ca has both sounds of c in one word: the first is an s across Latin America and a th in most of Spain, the second is always a k.

variations.display: La tienda está cerca de aquí
variations.cue: The shop is near here
variations.changed: "here" instead of a named place

variations.display: Mi casa está cerca de la tienda
variations.cue: My house is near the shop
variations.changed: turn it around — the same de holds

mistake.display: La tienda está cerca mi casa
mistake.why: cerca needs its de before naming what it is near: cerca de mi casa.

sentences.mnemonic: cerca de — near OF, every time.

sentences.display: Hay una tienda cerca de aquí
sentences.glossEn: lit. "There-is a shop near of here"
sentences.literal: There-is a shop near of here

words.note: "Here". It needs no preposition of its own — but a compound preposition keeps its de in front of it: cerca de aquí.

sentences.trap: hay, not está: you are telling someone a shop exists, not placing a shop they already know about. Swap in está and the sentence is asking to be finished with which shop.
sentences.sound: a-QUÍ. The qu is a plain k — the u is silent — and the accent puts the stress on the last syllable.

variations.display: ¿Hay una tienda cerca de aquí?
variations.cue: Is there a shop near here?
variations.changed: the question a traveller actually asks

variations.display: Hay un baño cerca de aquí
variations.cue: There's a bathroom near here
variations.changed: swap what you are looking for

mistake.display: Hay la tienda cerca de aquí
mistake.why: hay never takes la. Either Hay una tienda, or La tienda está cerca de aquí.

sentences.usage: Asking for, or giving, directions in the street.
sentences.mnemonic: aquí is here; allí is there — and both keep the de of cerca de.

words.note: The room, and the polite way to ask for it in any Spanish-speaking country. Masculine: el baño. The ñ is the ny of "canyon".

sentences.trap: Both speakers know there is a bathroom, so this is está and not hay. ¿Hay un baño aquí? is a different question — it asks whether one exists at all.
sentences.sound: BA-ño. Two syllables, and the ñ carries its own little y sound with it.

variations.display: ¿Hay un baño aquí?
variations.cue: Is there a bathroom here?
variations.changed: hay, because you do not know that one exists

variations.display: El baño está al lado de la puerta
variations.cue: The bathroom is next to the door
variations.changed: the answer

mistake.why: The bathroom's place is estar: ¿Dónde está el baño?

sentences.usage: The most useful sentence in the module, and possibly the level.
sentences.mnemonic: ¿Dónde está el baño? Learn it whole.

sentences.display: Mi casa está cerca del parque
sentences.cue: My house is near the park
sentences.glossEn: lit. "My house is-at near of-the park"
sentences.literal: My house is near of-the park

words.note: Park. Masculine — el parque — which is exactly why the de in front of it turns into del.

sentences.trap: cerca de la casa but cerca del parque. Nothing changed except the gender of the noun: de + el is always del, and de + la is always two words.
sentences.sound: PAR-que. The r is one tap, the qu is a k, and the final e is a clean short e — never the "ay" an English speaker expects.

variations.display: Mi casa está cerca de la tienda
variations.cue: My house is near the shop
variations.changed: feminine noun, so no contraction

variations.display: El parque está cerca de mi casa
variations.cue: The park is near my house
variations.changed: turn it around

mistake.display: Mi casa está cerca de el parque
mistake.why: de and el must fuse: cerca del parque.

sentences.mnemonic: de + el = del. Only with el.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to the park

words.note: a + el, fused. It is not a new word, it is the only shape those two are allowed to take together: voy al parque, never *voy a el parque. In front of a feminine noun nothing happens — voy a la tienda.

sentences.trap: M6's plan a and this destination a are the same one-letter word. It fuses with el only when a real el follows: voy al parque, but voy a trabajar keeps the a alone because a verb has no article.
sentences.sound: One syllable, AL, and it runs straight into the next word: voy-al-PAR-que.

variations.display: Mañana voy a la tienda
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to the shop
variations.changed: feminine — a la, with nothing fused

variations.display: Voy al baño
variations.cue: I'm going to the bathroom
variations.changed: another masculine place

mistake.why: a el is never written. It is al: voy al parque.

sentences.mnemonic: a + el = al. One letter each, one word out.
